claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
Combining Jev's reasoning with Pulumi makes the gap between designing ideal infrastructure and deploying it to production practically vanish.
In the past, having more infrastructure choices usually meant more complexity and technical debt.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one per geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
GeoDeploy is an example project hosted at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.

A GeoDeploy deployment request has four parts: target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule of EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max provider count, budget).

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math but makes no judgment calls; Jev decides region and modules but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS and decides nothing.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure when enumerating candidate regions.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS via Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev's choice() picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() rates something against a rubric the user describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, a hallucinated region like us-west-9 or made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

GeoDeploy's Jev call asks for one region selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency and capacity), and a fallback region (choice).
The file packages/decide/src/questions.ts in GeoDeploy contains buildStageAQuestions, importing choice, noul, and score from "@typesafe-ai/sdk".
TypeSafe advises to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing rubrics.

GeoDeploy's coverage rubric has 10 levels running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
The TypeSafeClient exposes a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers with fields such as selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because ranking weights live in code, GeoDeploy can re-tune ranking without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profile values: latency-optimized {cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12}; balanced {0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.12, 0.18}; residency-first {0.12, 0.12, 0.38, 0.23, 0.15}; failure-domain {0.08, 0.17, 0.48, 0.15, 0.12}.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), leaving Jev to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for a new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human); region when stack exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor for region pick, residency, or capacity 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
GeoDeploy's residency check lives in packages/decide/src/engine.ts and hard-rejects below 0.95 by throwing AiPathAborted, also throwing if the selection is not a known candidate id.
Each AiPathAborted in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

In GeoDeploy self-driving mode (`geodeploy monitor`), the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with answers no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check; code computes node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency and error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
GeoDeploy is released as open source.
GeoDeploy is open source as of this post's publication.
The Pulumi Automation API is documented at /docs/iac/automation-api/ and linked as /automation/.
